description: Peninsular rivers are primarily seasonal and heavily dependent on rainfall. Compared to the Himalayan rivers, they are much older, broader, have shallow valleys, and flow with a lower gradient.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Characteristics
sections.description: Understanding the main geographical features and terminology of the Peninsular drainage system.

key_concepts.explanation: A triangular landform created by deposition of alluvial soil at the mouth of a river as it enters the sea. Most East-flowing peninsular rivers (like Godavari, Krishna) form extensive deltas in the Bay of Bengal.
A partially enclosed coastal body of brackish water where a river meets the sea without forming a delta. West-flowing rivers (like Narmada, Tapi) empty into the Arabian Sea through estuaries.

A linear-shaped lowland between several highlands or mountain ranges created by the action of a geologic rift. The Narmada and Tapi rivers flow through rift valleys between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.

important_facts.fact: The Western Ghats act as the principal 'Water Divide' in Peninsular India, separating the west-flowing rivers from the east-flowing ones.

sections.title: Major East-Flowing Rivers - Part 1
sections.description: Detailed overview of the Godavari and Mahanadi river systems flowing into the Bay of Bengal.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: It is the longest peninsular river (1465 km). Due to its size and extent, it is often called the 'Dakshin Ganga' or 'Vridha Ganga' (Old Ganga). Major tributaries: Wainganga, Penganga, Indravati, and Pranhita.
It flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha, forming a massive delta before draining into the Bay of Bengal. Major tributaries: Seonath, Hasdeo, Mand, Ib, and Jonk.

sections.title: Major East-Flowing Rivers - Part 2
sections.description: Detailed overview of the Krishna and Cauvery river systems flowing into the Bay of Bengal.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: It is the second-largest peninsular river (1400 km) after the Godavari. Major tributaries: Tungabhadra, Bhima, Musi, Koyna, and Ghataprabha.

Often referred to as the 'Ganges of the South'. It is unique among peninsular rivers as it is almost perennial, receiving rainfall from both the South-West and North-East monsoons. Major tributaries: Amaravati, Bhavani, Hemavati, and Kabini.

sections.title: Major West-Flowing Rivers
sections.description: Rivers that drain into the Arabian Sea, characterized by flowing through rift valleys and forming estuaries.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: The longest west-flowing peninsular river. It creates the famous 'Marble Rocks' gorge and the Dhuandhar Falls near Jabalpur.
Known as the 'Twin of Narmada', it flows in a rift valley parallel to the Narmada, south of the Satpura range.
It is uniquely known as the only river in India that cuts across the Tropic of Cancer twice.

sections.title: Important Dams and River Projects
sections.description: Crucial multi-purpose river valley projects built across the major peninsular rivers.

key_associations.extra_info: It holds the record for being the longest earthen dam in India.
One of India's largest water resources projects, significant for both power generation and irrigation.
It is recognized as the world's largest and tallest masonry dam.
It is one of the largest dams in India and creates the Stanley Reservoir.
Also known as the Vallabh Sagar, it is the second-largest reservoir in Gujarat after the Sardar Sarovar.
